reason: This passage from Genesis 32-33 emphasizes and reinforces strict hierarchy throughout. Jacob carefully arranges his wives and children in explicit hierarchical order (maidservants first, then Leah and her children, then Rachel and Joseph—the beloved wife and preferred son last). He bows seven times before his elder brother Esau and consistently refers to himself as Esau's servant, using highly deferential language ('my lord,' 'your servant'). The passage demonstrates Jacob's patriarchal authority over his entire household and shows clear deference to both familial hierarchy (older brother) and divine hierarchy (angels and God). While the wrestling scene with the divine being shows Jacob's strength in struggle, he is physically injured in the encounter (his hip is dislocated), which actually reinforces rather than challenges the superiority of the divine. Nowhere in the text is strict hierarchy presented as unimportant or discouraged.
